abstract: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) is the most common metastatic skin cancer, with poor prognosis of metastatic disease. We investigated the role of the complement axis C3a/C3aR1 in CSCC progression. C3aR1 mRNA levels were elevated in CSCC tumors in vivo compared with normal skin. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed C3aR1 expression in macrophages within CSCCs. In 3D spheroid co-cultures of CSCC cells, fibroblasts, and macrophages, RNA sequencing showed increased C3aR1 mRNA expression in the presence of M2-like macrophages. Immunofluorescence staining localized C3aR1-expressing cells predominantly at the peripheral region of spheroids. Recombinant C3a enhanced CSCC cell invasion, whereas C3aR1 inhibitor SB290157 inhibited their invasion in co-culture with fibroblasts and macrophages. Immunohistochemistry of normal skin, actinic keratoses, CSCC in situ, CSCC, and metastases demonstrated C3aR1 expression on tumor cells in a subset of metastatic CSCCs and metastases. All C3aR1-positive primary tumors were high-risk (Clark level V; AJCC stage III-IV). Multiplexed immunofluorescence showed that increase in C3aR1-positive tumor cells, M2-like macrophages, and cancer-associated fibroblasts in CSCC was associated with metastasis risk and poor disease-specific survival. These findings support a role for C3a/C3aR1 signaling in CSCC invasion and metastasis and identify C3aR1 as a potential therapeutic target in advanced disease.
